title: Triplets, and Everything Above Them
excerpt: 3 Sum, counting triplets under a target, the closest triplet and 4 Sum: fix a prefix, run the converging pair on what is left, and drop an exponent from every one of them.
seoTitle: 3 Sum, 4 Sum and Triplet Counting With Two Pointers
seoDescription: How fixing a prefix and running a converging pair solves 3 Sum, counting triplets under a target, the closest triplet and 4 Sum, with duplicate handling and the k-Sum generalisation.
keywords: count triplets with sum less than target

content.text: Two Sum on a sorted array is O(n). Three Sum looks like a different problem, and it is not: fix the first element, and what is left is Two Sum on the rest of the array with a smaller target. One loop wrapped around the pass from two pages ago takes the obvious O(n³) down to O(n²).

That is the whole idea of this page, and it keeps going. Four Sum fixes two elements and runs the same pair pass, giving O(n³) instead of O(n⁴). k-Sum is k-2 nested loops with the converging pair at the bottom. What changes between the variants is not the structure but the single line at the comparison - and that line is where the interesting problems live.

Sorting does two jobs here. It makes the pair pass valid, and it puts duplicates next to each other so they can be skipped, which is what stops the same triplet being reported three times over.
There are two separate duplicate skips, and both are needed. The one on the outer loop stops the same value of

starting the same search twice. The two inside the pair loop, after a hit, stop the same pair being re-reported. Miss either and the output fills with repeats; the usual patch is to dedupe the results afterwards, which works and is slower and hides the fact that the sort already solved it.
A useful early exit falls out of the sort as well. Once
is greater than zero, every value to its right is too, so no triplet from there on can sum to zero, and the loop can stop rather than continue.

in the worst case, which puts the whole thing back at O(n³). The counting version avoids that with the observation this problem is really about.

The count added is hi - lo, not hi - lo + 1. The partner at hi is already counted as part of the current triplet; the block being credited is the choices strictly between lo and hi, plus hi itself. Write it out on a three-element example once and it stops being something to memorise.

Now the target does not have to be hit, only approached: find the triplet whose sum is nearest to it. The pass is unchanged, and only the comparison changes - instead of testing for equality, keep the best distance seen so far and move the pointer that pushes the sum in the right direction.
There is one shortcut worth taking. A distance of zero cannot be beaten, so an exact hit can return immediately rather than finishing the scan.

This variant is the clearest illustration of why the technique is more than a trick for exact matches. A hash map answers "does this exact sum exist" and is useless here; the ordered scan answers "how close can we get", because the sort gives every step a direction to move in.

Four values near the 32-bit limit overflow a 32-bit sum, and the comparison then sends the pointers the wrong way. The C++ version above accumulates in a 64-bit type for that reason. It is a favourite way for an otherwise correct k-Sum solution to fail on the last hidden test case.

content.text: The pattern has a floor worth knowing. k-Sum by this method is O(n^(k-1)), and for 4 Sum there is a hash-based approach that reaches O(n²) by storing every pair sum, at the cost of O(n²) memory and considerably more care around duplicates. Below that, no method is known to do better, and the problem is one of the standard hard cases in fine-grained complexity.

questions.prompt: In 3 Sum, what are the two distinct duplicate skips for?

options.label: The outer one stops the same a[i] starting an identical search; the inner ones stop the same pair being reported twice
They are the same check written twice, and one can be removed
Both exist to keep the array sorted after a swap

questions.prompt: Counting triplets under a target: the sum at (i, lo, hi) is under the target. Why can hi - lo be added at once?

options.label: Every partner between lo and hi is at most a[hi], so every one of those triplets is also under the target
Because the array is sorted, so all remaining triplets qualify
Because hi - lo counts the elements still to be examined

questions.prompt: Why does 4 Sum guard its inner duplicate skip with j > i + 1 instead of j > 0?

options.label: The first j of a new i is allowed to repeat a value used by an earlier i, and j > 0 would wrongly skip it
To avoid reading a[j - 1] out of bounds
Because j starts at i + 1, so the two conditions are equivalent
